en: The Treatise on Contemplating the Mind, with Preface; also titled the Treatise on Boiling Milk.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhizhe of Tiantai Xiusen Temple.
Question: The Buddhist scriptures are immeasurable, and treatises are likewise exceedingly numerous. Those who propagate the Dharma are truly countless.
In this world,
there are no places where the multitudes who listen and receive [the teaching] do not exist;
thus, the rain of Dharma universally moistens the fourfold assembly.
The dew-like moisture brings benefit to the boundless.
What have you seen or heard that leads you to further seek benefit by composing this treatise?
The answer is:
As you have asked,
the Buddha’s sūtras are immeasurable and his treatises are also exceedingly numerous.
This matter is commonly known.
However, those who propagate the Dharma, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, often add water to the milk;
this causes those who listen and receive it to lose the true flavor of the Path.
The fourfold assembly has increasingly turned toward worldly indulgence,
causing those with faith to gradually diminish and their discourse to grow thin;
it is feared that the profound and vast Great Dharma will not remain for long.
Sentient beings lose the benefit of the True Dharma as their eyes of wisdom perish;
for this reason, a profound sorrow arises that is difficult to endure.
This is not merely because they are ordinary, shallow, of little learning, and of limited vision.
Desiring to assist the parrot,
he exerted the strength of his wings,
immediately relying upon the power of the Triple Gem.
Desiring to compose this treatise,
the questioner wishes to know the general intent of its author;
therein are two points.
First, one should reproach oneself for the sake of all students;
second, if the fourfold assembly outside [the monastic community] is able to believe and accept it, one may also transmit it.
To answer briefly, he spoke in verse:
The Great Master is about to enter parinirvāṇa; The Compassionate Father has left this bequest:
Cultivate the path through the four foundations of mindfulness And abide by the Vinaya.
We are not the Buddha’s true disciples If we do not keep this bequest in mind.
If one’s practice is lax, the Way will not arise within; if one is negligent in the precepts, one fears the three miserable realms.
Because you do not inquire into or contemplate the mind, you cause others' faith to gradually diminish.
A crow does not bestow the Way; how could it ever repay the kindness of a white dove?
It is not merely that the field is poor; If the rain of the Dharma,
which is the seed of equality, does not fall, The seeds of the Dharma will surely wither and dry up,
And each will lack provisions for future lives, Failing to attain the three benefits and falling into suffering.
The Great Dharma is about to collapse; alas, to witness such a thing!
For this reason, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
The equal and true realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) is without activity and cannot be reached by any means.
If one can inquire into and contemplate the mind, And can practice it and reach its realization, this is precisely the four foundations of mindfulness.
If one relies on the Vinaya precepts with urgency, there is the Path within;
If one is urgent regarding the precepts, one will be reborn among humans and devas.
These are the true sons of the Buddha; Not failing their compassionate father, they belong to the devas and nāgas.
All rejoice in celebration; how could anyone not be delighted?
They are able to repay the kindness of the white crow By universally bestowing food upon the crows.
Since there are excellent fertile fields,
And the seeds of the Dharma fall as timely rain with impartiality, The seeds of the Dharma all grow,
each providing for the future; All together they obtain the three benefits.
For this reason, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
Those who come seeking the Dharma, desiring to hear of the Unsurpassed Way, do not know to ask about contemplating the mind;
thus, the wisdom born of hearing will never arise.
To those who come seeking the Dharma, desiring to contemplate the unsurpassed path,
If they do not know to inquire about contemplating the mind, The wisdom born of reflection will never arise.
To those who come seeking the Dharma, desiring to cultivate the unsurpassed path...
If one does not know to inquire about contemplating the mind, The cultivation of wisdom will ultimately not be accomplished.
For all who come seeking the Dharma And wish to cultivate the four samādhis,
If they do not know to inquire about contemplating the mind, They will suffer in hardship and gain nothing.
Those who come seeking the Dharma listen much and acquire words, yet they do not know how to inquire or contemplate the mind; thus they have not attained true bliss.
Those who come seeking the Dharma practice samādhi and attain meditative concentration.
Not knowing to inquire about contemplating the mind, like blind meditation one sees nothing;
for all who come seeking the Dharma and wish to repent of their many sins,
not knowing to inquire about contemplating the mind, they will find it ultimately difficult to be liberated from their offenses.
Those who come seeking the Dharma, desiring to leave afflictions behind, do not know to inquire about contemplating the mind; thus their afflictions will never be extinguished.
Those who come seeking the Dharma do so fundamentally for the sake of benefiting others.
Not knowing to inquire about contemplating the mind,
one regresses and causes others to slander those who come seeking the Dharma; desiring to promote and manifest the Buddha-dharma,
yet not knowing to inquire about contemplating the mind, one retreats from the Great Practice and suffers loss.
Such manifold gains and losses cannot be fully set forth in verse;
since there is no one who awakens to these various gains and losses,
for this reason, the *Cittabhāvanā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Cultivation of Mind) must be composed.
In this final age, those who cultivate the contemplative mind may attain perverse concentration,
giving rise to visions and inexhaustible eloquence; they claim for themselves to be treasures of the human world,
yet none recognize them— only their wild and solitary breath strikes the eyes.
Lifting their tails and walking on all fours, they fall into pits one after another;
for this reason, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*,
guard the breath at the bridge of the nose through *ānāpāna*, and cultivate the contemplation of impurity.
Though one attains the four dhyānas through ānāpāna, one cannot escape the karma of the hells;
To claim impurity is the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is a concealment;
Accepting a woman’s meal while in the bowl leads to rebirth according to one's dhyāna; Yet falling into the long-lived heavens is a difficulty.
For these reasons, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* (Cittaviveka-śāstra) and apply the mind according to the principles of actual phenomena.
If one lacks wisdom and gives rise to a demonic concentration (*bhūta-samādhi*) that manifests as a mind moving objects, such occurrences will destroy the Buddha-dharma.
At the end of his life, he was reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
The *Jiǔwǔjuànshǔ xiàngfǎ juéyí míng* (The Clarification of Doubts Regarding the Image Dharma with Its Ninety-five Retinues) states:
"Because the three masters destroyed the Buddha-dharma for these reasons and conditions, one must compose the *Guānxīn lùn* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind)."
With no inner inclination toward the Path, they harbor crooked and flattering thoughts of fame and profit;
falsely manifesting the appearance of meditative sitting, they seek renown, gain, and followers,
thereby corrupting the minds of others and destroying the Buddha’s True Dharma.
This is Śāṇḍila, who through these causes and conditions will fall into the Avīci Hell after death;
for this reason, one must compose the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind),
and by expounding the Dharma, liberation shall be attained— this applies equally to the assembly that listens to the Dharma.
The questioner asks about contemplating the mind, yet it is like a poor man counting another’s treasures.
The speaker answers about contemplating the mind, yet without speaking, there is no instruction.
The listener asks about contemplating the mind, yet without questioning, there is nothing to be attained.
For this reason, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*;

the precepts are for the purpose of restraining the horse of the mind. Though one may uphold the five divisions of the Vinaya, if one does not know to inquire about contemplating the mind, the horse of the mind will never be tamed.
The Vinaya sustains the Buddha-dharma; One who understands the external but not the internal is rebuked by the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.
Only one who is thus called a true upholder of the Vinaya, For these reasons, must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
Reciting the sutras brings liberation, not for the sake of worldly wealth or profit.
If one can inquire into the contemplation of the mind, one will break open a single atom to reveal a great thousand-fold world-system of sutra scrolls;
one should receive, uphold, read, and recite this.
Hearing and retaining [the teachings] without forgetfulness, The mind opens and attains liberation;
for these causes and conditions, One must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
Rather than contemplating others or practicing offerings, One should promote and manifest the path for those who practice with peace.
The secret mind seeks self-benefit; relying on it for sustenance, one destroys others’ joy and abandons goodness.
Like a camel or a donkey used to repay a person, if one can inquire into and observe the mind, one will be just like Bhadra the camel.
For these reasons, I have composed the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.

Each of the various paths has its own methods; yet, though I have long scrutinized and investigated them without exception, I have suddenly caught a glimpse of the teachings of Śākyamuni, which took me many years to fully comprehend.
Not only are those teachings clumsy, but there is also a mind intent on subversion;
this is the work of Kapila. How could a sage and seer tolerate such a thing?
For these reasons, one must compose the *Cittabhāvanā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Cultivation of the Mind).
To possess wealth and honor yet lack the Way leads only to the increase of arrogance and heedlessness;
if one can inquire and contemplate the mind, one attains the true riches of the Dharma.
Thus, though high, one does not fall into peril; though full, one does not overflow.
Not attached to worldly wealth and honor, with the mind always dwelling upon the Way and the Dharma—for these causes and conditions—one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
The poor and lowly are full of guile and flattery; they spy and look for opportunities to commit manifold evils.
Now you are subjected to the laws of kings, And upon death, will fall into the three evil realms.
If you can inquire into the contemplation of the mind, Then you will find peace on the path of nourishing greed.
To have the Way is true nobility; To be unconditioned is true wealth and joy.
For these reasons, one must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
All members of the fourfold assembly are children of the Buddha; there are none who are not kin to the Dharma.
Yet, by disputing over the wholesome Dharma out of attachment, they instead bind themselves in enmity for the future.
If one can inquire into the contemplation of the mind,
All who are like the offspring of lions, blending together like water and milk, And who are entirely of the sandalwood forest—
For these reasons, one must compose the *Treatise on the Contemplation of the Mind*.
Years decline and the body bears disease; the eyes grow dim and the ears gradually go deaf.
The mind becomes clouded with frequent forgetfulness; each year is not like the one before.
King Death is like a golden-winged bird; before long, he will swallow up the very root of life.
Once the cords of karma are severed, how could one speak when breath has ceased?
For this reason, I must compose the *Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*.
I prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions and to those who contemplate the mind with deep compassion.
Exhorting the virtuous to observe with clarity, To give rise to the sublime bliss of perfect enlightenment—
I bow my head to those who contemplate the mind with profound compassion.
Exhorting the virtuous to observe with clarity, They shall attain the true Dharma and escape suffering.
I prostrate to the Sangha of the ten directions, who, through skillful observation,
enter the great ocean of harmony; with immeasurable joy,
I prostrate to the Master Nāgārjuna, and pray that he will look upon those who contemplate the mind.
May they quickly attain clear understanding; Furthermore, may they cultivate the three minds of equanimity.
Now, by the power of the Triple Gem, I shall raise thirty-six questions.
Regarding their gateways and various subtle gateways, The specific instances are too numerous to count.
If one can contemplate the mind of a single thought-moment and answer this question,
know that the eye of wisdom has opened and one has entered the Cool Lake;
if one cannot answer this question, alas, how blind and ignorant one is!
If even the lesser meaning is not seen, how can one practice the Great Way?
Alas! In the age of the Final Dharma, there shall be none who attain the Way.
Even if there were three or four such people, how could they possibly distinguish this question?
Therefore, with a heart of compassion, I take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Having composed this *Tarkajvālā* (The Lamp of Reasoning), may those who contemplate it attain clarity;
and may all who see or hear it never give rise to doubt or slander.
"Faithfully accepting and diligently practicing, one will surely obtain the Dharma of great benefit.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"For what reason is this question posed in the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa*?"
The answer is:

Those people in the final age who count their treasures out of greed have no business with these words; they apply them only to those who sit in meditation and contemplate practice, settling the mind upon the nose-tip and the impurity of *ānāpāna*.
This, too, is like facing a wall;
how can one discuss the Way?
There are those who contemplate the mind, enter the Way, and attain meditative concentration, yet give rise to perverted understandings.
His eloquence was inexhaustible,
and he considered himself a treasure of the human world;
yet how could he have known that his heterodoxy and arrogance were burning so fiercely?
I now pose this question:
if you do not understand each and every sentence,
how can you claim what you have not attained as attained, or what you have not realized as realized?
In the "Exhortation to Uphold" chapter of the Lotus Sutra,
the Buddha says that such a person is difficult to transform and deliver.
Furthermore, in the "Never-Disparaging" chapter...
After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound passed into extinction,
such human beings as these were exceedingly numerous, not just one or two.
Furthermore, I feel deep sorrow and lamentation.
The disciples of this house have followed him for many years, and having observed the mind for some time,
they have consequently failed to inquire into it through such rigorous investigation; thus,
they remain unstained by internal dharmas.
They wrote down foreign scripts;
they surreptitiously took notes and hurried about,
carrying sutras and śāstras as they wandered aimlessly.
Why not bestow your speech so that we may open a single atom to read the great scroll of the sūtras?
Alas, I have followed this deluded disciple for many years,
yet I have gained nothing at all.
If one were suddenly to close one's eyes in death, who then would show them the way?
For this reason, my grief has become even more intense;
thus, I have composed this treatise.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* elucidates the gateway of the forty-two letters.
It begins by stating:
"If one hears the letter A-gate..."
This immediately explains all meanings,
namely that all phenomena are originally unarisen.
Nāgārjuna also composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* as a commentary on the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*.
With correct intention, one does not initiate a discussion on the eight points, such as non-arising and so forth.
To explain "initial non-arising" by means of a single verse, it says:
"All phenomena do not arise from themselves."
Nor does it arise from another;
it is neither co-existent nor causeless.
Therefore, it is said to be unarisen.
Now, focusing solely on the first phrase,
"arising from itself," thirty-six questions are raised.
If one is able to answer these questions within the contemplation of the mind without any obstruction, [one has attained proficiency].
It should be known that these six types of practitioners enter the practice of contemplation therein;
among the five grades of disciples, they enter the initial stage of the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*).
Thus, the Sūtra says:
Even upon hearing a single verse,
one penetrates immeasurable meanings and explains them in succession according to the Dharma.
From months, four months, to a year.
The Treatise says:
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself, why are the four [factors] not mentioned?
Free from conceptual proliferation, attachment, and contention, with a mind as pure as space, I ask:
regarding this self-arisen mind, how is it bound by the afflictions that are the activities of Māra,
and why is it scorched by the burning house of the three realms?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—what are the various views, afflictions, and karmas of the non-Buddhists that cause one to transmigrate through the six realms?
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—what are the three vehicles?
The clumsy means sever the views and afflictions, Emerging from the burning house of the triple world;
Ask about the contemplation that gives rise to the mind:
How is it that the skillful means of the three vehicles do not sever the fetters, Yet attain entry into the two types of nirvana?

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how is it that in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), one seeks the constant fruit of the Mahāyāna? How does a Bodhisattva sever the delusions specific to each stage?
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how is it in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao)?
Without destroying the dharma-realm, one abides in the nirvāṇa of the three virtues.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself: how does one attain nirvāṇa?
By practicing the four kinds of samādhi, one attains the true patience of non-arising.
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one skillfully accomplish the twenty-five expedient means?
How does one discipline the mind to enter the right path?
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one know the causes and conditions?
Arising from ten kinds of objects, One accomplishes the three wisdoms within a single mind.

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the self-arising mind, how does one know that each of the ten objects accomplishes the ten dharma-vehicles, and thus wanders joyfully through the four quarters?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind that arises of itself—
how does one abide in no-dharmas when entering the first stage of the Bodhisattva path,
and how does one accomplish the six perfections throughout the forty-two stages?
One is able to attain all samādhis and all dhāraṇīs.
Regarding the inquiry into the mind that arises of itself: how does one obtain the six supernormal powers?
How does one transform through the four kinds of conduct? What are the four analytical knowledges and the four hindrances?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how are the marks and signs attained so as to become the two Buddhas, the True and the Responsive?
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself in response to conditions like a mirror image—how does one come to possess the ten powers?
And the four fearlessnesses— Shining inwardly and outwardly, perfectly round.
Question: Regarding the contemplation that arises from within the mind itself, how can one contemplate the mind so as to attain the eighteen unique qualities not shared with the world?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one attain great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness?
How does one have compassion for sentient beings without perceiving signs of difference?
Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—what are the skillful means?
To bring all sentient beings to fulfillment and to adorn and purify all buddha-fields—
how does one contemplate the mind that arises of itself?
How does one adorn the Bodhi tree within a single mind and establish the pure site of enlightenment?

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the self-arising mind—how does one sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and manifest the four modes of attaining Buddhahood? How does one respond to sentient beings without error or gradation?
Regarding the contemplation of the self-arising mind—how does one turn the four teachings?
The pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma, from which all attain the nectar of immortality— I ask:
how does the self-arising mind manifest the four Buddhas and the four aspects of nirvāṇa?
May I ultimately know this without remainder.

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how is it known that the four lands of the environment and its inhabitants share the same celestial vessel, yet the color of the food differs?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one relate to this mind?
Beholding all faculties and conditions, you penetrate them without obstruction.
Questioning the observation of the self-arising mind, how do you know the *siddhānta*—
formless and without objective referent— yet manifesting forms to preach the Dharma extensively?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one know the gradual, sudden, secret, and indeterminate teachings?
How does one know these four teachings through the single sound?
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind arising from itself—how does one know the four teachings?
Each opens four gates, as do all the dharma-gates;
Inquiring into the contemplation of the mind that arises of itself:
How does one compose a treatise that penetrates the various scriptures Through the four teachings, the four gates, and the sixteen gates?

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the self-arising mind—how does one abide in the concentration of wisdom and universally enter the ten dharma-realms? How does one extensively benefit all sentient beings?
Regarding the contemplation of the self-arising mind—how does one know the four lands?
Because the teachings have increases and decreases, To universally benefit all sentient beings,
one asks: How does one know that this mind inherently possesses all Buddha-dharmas,
such that not a single dharma exists outside of the mind?

Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind that arises from itself—how does one know that this mind is the equal Dharma-realm? Question: Regarding the contemplation of the mind that arises from itself—how does one know this mind? [The Buddha] does not deliver sentient beings. Question:
Regarding the contemplation of the mind that arises from itself—how does one know this mind?
The Dharma-realm is like space, ultimately beyond all thought.
When one asks about observing the mind that arises of itself, how can there be words?
All speech is cut off; it is tranquil and beyond verbal expression.
Now, based on observing the mind that arises spontaneously within a single thought-moment,
thirty-six questions will be briefly raised.
These concern those who externally observe the mind, as well as those long-term associates who practice the four kinds of samādhis.
If that practitioner of mind-observation can penetrate each and every [aspect] thoroughly,
they should conceive of the mind as the Buddha, drawing near to it and practicing in accordance with the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
If their disciples and retinue likewise remain unimpeded in this regard, [they shall attain liberation].
This is the practice of true causes;
these are the true descendants of the Dharma Prince,
who succeed the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall never be severed.
If one cannot, within the observation of a single thought-moment, answer this question for each and every thought as it arises,
then one is a member of the retinue of celestial Māras and non-Buddhists,
driven about by them.
This is because they currently reside within the prison of the triple world and have not yet found a way to escape it.
If their minds do not seek to exert themselves toward liberation,
they will inevitably fall into the pits of the three vehicles or the three evil realms.
To sever for oneself the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body and to annihilate the retinue of Bodhi is truly to destroy the kingdom of the Buddha-dharma.
The Mahāyāna family has already perished.
Alas, alas! To know [this]—what is it but a great calamity?
If one contemplates that the mind arises from itself, gain and loss are as described above;
it is the same when contemplating arising from another, arising from both, or arising without a cause.
Within the gateway of conforming characteristics, there is attachment to sounds and forms.
Within the gateway of adverse signs, whether numerical or non-numerical,
one who refuses to comply with the signs shall enter hell;
it is difficult to cross over the intermediate realm of the three worlds.
Deliverance and non-deliverance are wondrous and difficult to conceive;
those whose deluded minds follow after appearances harbor many doubts.
They refuse to take the priceless medicine of *amṛta* (clarified butter).
If one asks how the deluded mind can thus enter nirvana,
it is further revealed that within the gate of characteristics (lakṣaṇamukha), four and three [categories] are taught.
The three wheels and four teachings are explained according to sentient dispositions.
Unwilling to follow one another into the Avīci hell,
they cause the five parts to seek out their traces;
yet these are neither traces nor distance, nor are they the five parts.
The three truths and three contemplations are contained therein;
yet ordinary minds cannot skillfully resolve them.
With blind hearts clinging to views, they all claim that everything is empty.
Within the gateway of hidden characteristics, form and color are transcended;
through the twelve gateways of the harmonization of the three and four,
one refuses to follow worldly sentiments or give rise to craving and attachment.
If one employs skillful means to destroy the enemy of Māra,
then craving— the enemy Māra— is the Mother of the Buddhas;
she is also the profound primordial limit of the three bodies.
Each establishes names according to their own inclinations;
some call it the "five hidden marks," yet starving oneself all day long is not true moderation in eating.
Enduring cold all day long is not asceticism; being frugal all day long does not contradict greed.
Practicing compassion all day long while taking the lives of others;
fearing punishment all day long while turning toward unwholesome deeds.
Seeking physicians all day long only increases the illness;
practicing generosity all day long only increases stinginess;
severing anger all day long only causes the three poisons to flourish.
Inconceivable, truly inconceivable!
The full moon remains constant, neither waxing nor waning; yet the deluded minds of ordinary beings perceive it as increasing and decreasing.
Even if its returning light were to shine upon the Western Regions, its underlying principle would never shift.
Skillfully employing skillful means to deliver beings, Neither creating enemies nor becoming the Dharma-body of the Buddha;
The skillful application of the wondrous is inconceivable— I ask: from where does this certainty emerge?
*Treatise on Contemplating the Mind*, one fascicle.
